agent_notes: The superscription is verse 1 in the Hebrew (KJV 102:0, a heading). I treat it as text, not as editorial title. The usual translation 'when he is overwhelmed' for כי יעטף is a gloss; 'when he faints/wraps himself' is the literal sense. STEPBible has 'if' for כי; I read it as 'when' (so ASV, KJV, Webster; YLT 'when he is feeble').

Commentators split on who speaks: Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Malbim read the psalm as the voice of the exiles; Meiri also records a view that it is David's. I did not decide this in the translation and kept the first person singular.
שקוי has an unusual spelling with vav; Radak discusses its vocalization and Meiri notes that some grammarians read it as if it had two yods (שקויי). I glossed the form as it stands, 'my drinks'.

history.note: [consider] Attribute the taste reading to Radak and Metzudat David, and to Ibn Ezra only the figurative reading. (PS.102.10 packet, Ibn Ezra: "דרך משל, כמו: הכפישני באפר".)

agent_notes: STEPBible gives 'you have picked up me' for נשאתני; I corrected to 'you lifted me up' since it contrasts with 'and you threw me down' (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat David, Malbim all read raised-then-flung). Radak adds the image of lifting something high to drop it harder.

כצל נטוי: nātûy is a passive participle of נטה, 'stretched out, extended'. KJV 'that declineth' follows the sense 'lengthening toward evening' (Rashi, Radak, Meiri). I kept 'stretched out' in the literal and 'lengthening' in the dramatic layer. The word 'declineth' is therefore interpretive in KJV and ASV.

agent_notes: The subject of עִנָּה is not stated. Rashi supplies 'my enemy', tying the verse to the complaint of vv. 11-12. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David also read the enemy. The reading of God as subject follows the parallel with v. 11 ('you have lifted me up and thrown me down') and is my own; the dramatic layer keeps the subject unnamed so as to hold both. Ketiv/Qere: the packet marks כֹּחִי as Q(K) without showing the written form, so the gloss follows the reading and the note does not name the Ketiv.

agent_notes: Hebrew has אֹמַר, an imperfect: 'I say' / 'I would say', not the past tense of KJV/ASV 'I said'. I kept the present in both layers; BBE 'I will say' and YLT 'I say' agree. STEPBible glosses אֵלִי 'O God my' and the entity link points to YHWH; I glossed it 'my God', as a vocative address to the one the psalm calls YHWH in v.13 ff.

The Targum's 'bring me to the world to come' has no counterpart in the Hebrew; I cite it only as a reading of 'lift up', not as the sense of the Hebrew. Rashi reads the 'I' as Israel as a whole ('us'), Metzudat David as all generations; the Hebrew is singular, and the psalm's heading makes it an individual's lament, so the commentary notes both.

Last verb יַחֲלֹפוּ is a jussive-looking form after an imperfect: 'and they pass on / are changed'. KJV 'they shall be changed' hides that it is the same root חלף as 'you change them': the clothing is swapped, and so the heavens 'pass on'. I repeated 'change' in the literal layer to keep the wordplay. STEPBible gloss 'they may pass away' corrected to 'and they are changed' because it must echo תַּחֲלִיפֵם.
Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Ibn Ezra disagree on whether the heavens and earth really perish or only change; the commentary states the Hebrew's two verbs (אבד, חלף) and does not choose a cosmology.

אַתָּה־הוּא: five English versions all say 'the same'. It is the idiom of the 'I am he' formula (Deut 32:39, Isa 43:10, 41:4), and I note it as my own reading, without a source citation. The Septuagint and Hebrews 1:12 render it 'the same'; I mention Hebrews 1:10-12 because the quotation of vv.26-28 there is well known.

יִכּוֹן is singular (Niphal of כון) after the plural-sounding 'offspring'; זֶרַע is a collective. BBE 'a safe resting-place' for יִשְׁכּוֹנוּ is looser than the Hebrew, which is the plain verb 'dwell/settle'; I follow KJV's sense of lasting residence but keep 'dwell' to preserve the שכן / Shekhinah-root echo only as a mention, not a claim.

STEPBible lemma H4168 מוֹקֵד and gloss 'a hearth' for קֵד: the form is the shortened 'ked' of מוֹקֵד after כְּמוֹ. Ibn Ezra counts it as the two-word reading 'כמו קד' (his remark 'שתים'); Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as one word 'כמוקד', the place where the fire burns. The Masoretic division is כְּמוֹ־קֵד, kept in the literal layer. KJV 'hearth' is right; ASV/YLT 'firebrand' is a different reading.

Radak and Meiri note the spelling הוּכָּה with vav and dagesh (a 'strange' form of the pual/hophal). I corrected STEPBible 'it has been struck' to 'it has been struck down', since the following 'like vegetation' points to sun-struck grass (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David).
מֵאֲכֹל is 'from eating' (privative min), 'I forgot away from eating'. KJV 'so that I forget to eat' makes it a result clause; the Hebrew has 'for' (כי).

agent_notes: קאת and כוס appear together in Lev 11:17-18 and Deut 14:16-17; the identification is uncertain (pelican, cormorant, little owl, tawny owl). I used 'desert owl' and 'ruin owl' and kept the Hebrew in notes. Radak and Meiri say both birds have a mournful cry (קול נהי). Malbim reads קאת as a fish-eating bird (pelican type).

Meaning of שקדתי: 'I lie awake' (Targum: all night; STEPBible 'wakeful') versus Metzudat Zion 'I hurried', and Radak 'I was busy/persistent'. I chose the common 'I keep watch / lie awake'. צפור is a generic bird; the Hebrew has no 'sparrow'. KJV and Webster 'sparrow' narrows it; YLT, BBE 'bird' is right.

נשבעו בי is the hard clause. Rashi, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David: enemies use the speaker as a formula of oath/curse ('may I be like him'; cf. Isa 65:15, Num 5:21). KJV/Webster 'sworn against me' and YLT 'sworn against me' blur this; ASV 'do curse by me' and BBE are closer. מהוללי is a polel participle of הלל I (to be mad, to rave), not הלל 'to praise'; STEPBible 'those who mock' is Rashi's sense.

В еврейской нумерации заглавие — стих 1, поэтому в Синодальном переводе (Пс 101) нумерация сдвинута на единицу; здесь следуем еврейской. «Страждущий» (ани) — как в Синодальном; «унывает» для яʼатоф в драматическом слое заменено образом изнеможения, а в буквальном сохранено «обёртывается/изнемогает».
